# About the author {.unnumbered}

![](images/dave-parr.jpg){fig-alt="Dave Parr" width="200" style="float: right; margin: 0 0 1rem 1.5rem; border-radius: 50%;"}

I'm **Dr. David Parr**, a Teaching Assistant Professor in the Department of Geography and the Environment at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. I teach classes in spatial data science, GIS, programming, web mapping, spatial databases, cartography, spatial modeling and analysis, and data acquisition and integration.

I see my disciplines, Geographic Information Science (GIS) and spatial data science, as the intersections of Geography and Computer Science, the fields in which I have earned my degrees. I want students to be able to *think geographically*: to critically consider the dynamic spatial and temporal issues of a problem, and to consider how scale and distance affect our human and physical environments. I also want them to *think computationally*: to break problems into smaller components in a logical sequence, and to consider how a representation in a computer is related to the object in the real world. These skills, understanding spatial relations and logical problem solving, are critical in our discipline and in the wider world.

My teaching and research interests include volunteered geographic information, space-time spatial analysis and modeling, GIS and geography education, and GIS and society, including digital places and web GIS.

## About this book

This book was developed and written from several years of lectures for GEOG 215. It is a [Quarto](https://quarto.org) book: every chapter is a runnable document, so the tables, maps, and figures come from the R code printed beside them, and many code boxes can be edited and run right in your browser.

## About the cover

![](images/rastie.jpg){fig-alt="Oil-painting-style portrait of Rastie the Dragon, a friendly green dragon in a graduation cap and gown with a GIS@UNC emblem, seated in a study with globes, old books, and a world map, in an ornate gold frame" width="180" style="float: right; margin: 0 0 1rem 1.5rem;"}

The dragon on the cover is **Rastie**, the mascot of my textbooks. Rastie hatched one spring under a stack of old USGS topographic quadrangles in the basement of Carolina Hall and took their name from the first thing they ever learned to read: a raster grid. Like most dragons, Rastie keeps a hoard, but theirs is made of maps, globes, and well-documented datasets instead of gold, and they are happiest when every layer shares the same coordinate reference system. Rastie has sat in on GEOG 215, GEOG 370, and GEOG 491 more times than anyone can count, and the portrait here was painted to celebrate their graduation with a GIS@UNC degree. The cap still doesn't sit quite right between the horns.

On this book's cover, Rastie is at the keyboard writing R code, surrounded by charts, maps, and a few too many open scripts. Rastie also appears on the covers of the companion books, *Geographic Information Science* (GEOG 370) and *Principles of GIS* (GEOG 491).

The cover illustrations were generated by Google Gemini.
